01 / THE FRAMEWORK

A place for everything.
Nothing up its sleeve.

Good defaults without hidden machinery. Tsir gives your application a clear structure, so you can spend your time on the part that makes it yours.

  • ✓
    Typed from the boundary inward

    Validate requests before your handler sees them.

  • ✓
    Dependencies you can point to

    Constructor injection. No ambient service locator.

  • ✓
    Web standards, all the way through

    A standard Request goes in. A Response comes out.

Explore the HTTP pipeline →
Your application, explicitly.
TypeScript · HTTP
import { createFetchHandler } from '@tsir/http';
import { Controller, Get, RouteRegistry, compileRoutes } from '@tsir/router';

const registry = new RouteRegistry();

@Controller(registry, '/hello')
class HelloController {
  @Get('/')
  greet(): { message: string } {
    return { message: 'hello' };
  }
}

const handler = createFetchHandler(compileRoutes(registry.entries()));
const response = await handler(new Request('http://localhost/hello'));

console.log(response.status, await response.text());
TypeScript · Validation
import { z } from 'zod';
import { validate } from '@tsir/validate';

const Signup = z.object({
  email: z.string().email(),
  age: z.number().int().min(13),
});

const result = await validate(Signup, { email: 'not-an-email', age: 12 });

if (result.ok) {
  console.log(result.value.email);
} else {
  console.log(result.issues.map((issue) => issue.path.join('.')));
}
TypeScript · Database
import { type D1Like, createD1Driver, createDatabase, statement } from '@tsir/database';

const binding = {
  prepare: () => ({
    bind() {
      return this;
    },
    all: async () => ({ success: true, results: [{ one: 1 }] }),
    run: async () => ({ success: true, meta: { changes: 0 } }),
  }),
  batch: async () => [],
} as unknown as D1Like;

const database = createDatabase({ driver: createD1Driver({ binding }) });
const result = await database.query(statement('select 1 as one'));

console.log(result.rows);

02 / DATA & SECRETS

Your data.
Your database.
Your keys.

Keep the database tools you like. Add the boundaries your application needs. Tsir is honest about what each driver can do—and refuses what it cannot.

  • ✓
    No pretend transactions

    Real transactions on Postgres. Atomic batches on D1.

  • ✓
    Migrations with a paper trail

    Drizzle’s journal, drift checks and explicit rollback.

  • ✓
    Encryption that fails closed

    Column-bound envelopes and resumable key rotation.

Take a look at the data layer →

03 / CONNECT & DEPLOY

One application.
The right units.

HTTP handlers, background workers and scheduled jobs each have a job to do. Describe them once, review the graph, then build an artifact for each deploy unit.

  • ✓
    A graph you can review

    Unit boundaries and bindings are committed, not guessed.

  • ✓
    Capabilities checked first

    Unsupported bindings fail before a bundle is built.

OPINIONATED, NOT OPAQUE

A few things we won’t compromise.

01

Explicit over ambient

Dependencies arrive through constructors. Transactions are handles you pass, not context you inherit.

02

Compiled over discovered

Routes become an immutable table. Production boot reads data instead of scanning your classes.

03

Refusal over pretending

Missing keys fail closed. Unsupported capabilities fail early. The framework says what it cannot do.

04

Evidence over adjectives

Package claims come with tests and documented failure modes. No invented benchmarks or customer counts.
